lead: A Fourier transform turns a signal x(t) into a spectrum X(ω). Many operations that are hard in time become easy algebra in frequency. Shifting a signal adds a phase ramp. Convolving with an impulse response becomes multiplying spectra. Multiplying by a cosine copies and halves the spectrum. Engineers use these rules for filters, radio transmitters, sound tones, and power-supply noise checks. This chapter lists the main properties, proves the convolution and modulation theorems, and shows how to compute transforms without long integrals.
prereq: You need: 3.2 Fourier transform and the convolution integral from Unit 2.

blocks.where: x(t) is the signal; X(ω) is its spectrum; ω is angular frequency in rad/s; j is the imaginary unit.

blocks.text: The table gives the rules used most often. Here a and b are constants, t₀ is a time shift in seconds, a is nonzero, ω₀ is a frequency shift in rad/s, and δ is the unit impulse.

For real x(t), the spectrum obeys X(−ω)=X*(ω). The magnitude is even and the phase is odd. An even real signal has a real even spectrum. An odd real signal has an imaginary odd spectrum. These symmetry facts let you check an answer quickly.

sections.h3: Convolution theorem: time convolution becomes spectral product

blocks.text: Convolution in time is defined as y(t)=x(t)*h(t)=∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup>x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ. The convolution theorem says the transform of y(t) is the product of the two transforms.

blocks.where: x(t) is the input; h(t) is the impulse response; X(ω) and H(ω) are their spectra; * means convolution.

items: Substitute u=t−τ, so t=u+τ and dt=du.
The double integral separates into ∫x(τ)e<sup>−jωτ</sup>dτ times ∫h(u)e<sup>−jωu</sup>du.

blocks.text: The dual rule is multiplication in time: x(t)y(t) ↔ (1/2π)X(ω)*Y(ω). The factor 1/2π comes from the inverse-transform convention. This rule explains why a short window smears a spectrum.

sections.h3: Modulation theorem: cosine makes two shifted copies

blocks.text: Use Euler's identity cos(ω₀t)=(e<sup>jω₀t</sup>+e<sup>−jω₀t</sup>)/2. Multiply x(t) by this cosine. The frequency-shift rule gives one copy moved to ω₀ and one copy moved to −ω₀.

blocks.where: ω₀ is the carrier frequency in rad/s; X(ω) is the original spectrum; each shifted copy has half the original height.

blocks.text: The shift rule itself is e<sup>jω₀t</sup>x(t) ↔ X(ω−ω₀). The modulation theorem uses a cosine, so it applies two shifts. Some syllabi call modulation the frequency-shifting property. The cosine version is the one used for amplitude modulation.

A radio station multiplies voice by a carrier cosine. The voice spectrum moves to the carrier frequency. A receiver multiplies by a local cosine and moves it back. The half-size copies carry the same information.

figure.caption: The upper path shows a signal multiplied by a cosine: its spectrum splits into two half-size copies at plus and minus ω₀. The lower path shows convolution in time becoming multiplication of spectra.

spec.title: Two transform theorems
spec.aria: Multiplying a signal by a cosine shifts and halves its spectrum, while convolution in time becomes multiplication of spectra.

examples.question: Find the Fourier transform of x(t)=e<sup>−2t</sup>cos(10t)u(t), where t is in seconds and x(t) is in volts. Also give X(0) in V·s.
steps: Take the base signal g(t)=e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t). Its transform is G(ω)=1/(2+jω), with ω in rad/s.
Write x(t)=g(t)cos(10t). The carrier frequency is ω₀=10 rad/s.

w0 = 10.0
w = 0.0
X = 0.5*(1/(2 + 1j*(w - w0)) + 1/(2 + 1j*(w + w0)))
print(X.real)

traps: Wrong sign in frequency shift: e<sup>jω₀t</sup>x(t) shifts to X(ω−ω₀), not X(ω+ω₀).
Forgetting the 1/2π factor in the time-multiplication rule x(t)y(t) ↔ (1/2π)X(ω)*Y(ω).
Missing the 1/|a| factor in scaling: x(at) ↔ (1/|a|)X(ω/a).
Using X(ω)+H(ω) or X(ω)*H(ω) in frequency for time convolution; the correct result is the product X(ω)H(ω).
Wrong phase sign in time shift: x(t−t₀) gives e<sup>−jωt₀</sup>X(ω), not e<sup>+jωt₀</sup>X(ω).

quiz.q: State the modulation theorem for x(t)cos(ω₀t).
Why does the convolution theorem make LTI system analysis easier?
quiz.a: The output spectrum is Y(ω)=X(ω)H(ω). Multiply the input spectrum by the frequency response, then inverse-transform. No time convolution integral is needed.

quiz.q: If x(t) ↔ X(ω)=1/(1+jω), find the transform of x(t−2).

quiz.a: The base transform is 1/(2+jω). With ω₀=20, X(ω)=½[1/(2+j(ω−20))+1/(2+j(ω+20))].

quiz.q: A real signal has spectrum X(ω). Explain why |X(ω)| is even and ∠X(ω) is odd.
quiz.a: For real x(t), X(−ω)=X*(ω). Taking magnitudes gives |X(−ω)|=|X*(ω)|=|X(ω)|. The phase changes sign: ∠X(−ω)=−∠X(ω).

quiz.q: X(ω) is zero for |ω|>B. The signal is multiplied by cos(ω₀t). What spectral bands appear, and what condition avoids overlap?
quiz.a: The copies occupy [ω₀−B,ω₀+B] and [−ω₀−B,−ω₀+B]. They do not overlap when ω₀>B. Each copy has half the original height.

beyond: Not for the exam. In software radio, the modulation theorem moves baseband samples to a carrier and back using digital mixers. OFDM transmitters use inverse FFT, and fast filtering uses FFT convolution. Search 'digital upconversion', 'OFDM modulation', 'FFT convolution', and 'analytic signal'. Modern curricula connect these properties to the short-time Fourier transform and wavelets.
